report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) had high vaccination coverage, and few infections were reported prior to the establishment of the Omicron variant.

We investigated whether changes in the timing and rate of booster dose administration could have reduced severe disease outcome and reliance on non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) during the Omicron wave in NL.

We used a vaccination-stratified epidemiological model calibrated to serology data to investigate the impact of vaccination relative to counterfactual vaccination strategies under actual, strict and no NPI scenarios.

Compared with a Canadian vaccination rate scenario, the actual vaccination rollout in NL was estimated to have prevented approximately 519 hospitalizations and 122 deaths from December 15, 2021 to December 15, 2022, corresponding to reductions of 25.9% and 30.9%, respectively.

These reductions reflected contributions from NL's higher initial primary series coverage (81.3%), higher final booster dose coverage (57.3%), and the implementation of various NPIs for 89 days after the Omicron BA.1 variant became established.
Earlier and faster administration of booster doses reduced the duration of strict NPIs required to achieve hospitalization targets.
Our findings show how the timing and rate of vaccination rollout can complement NPIs to reduce severe disease and the duration for which strict NPIs are required.

Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) were implemented to control the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus and consisted of social distancing, gathering limits, and business and school closures (Brauner et al, 2021; Flaxman et al, 2020; Sonabend et al, 2021).

We investigate the effect of different vaccination rollout and NPI implementation strategies specifically for Omicron variant spread in the Canadian province of NL.

We focus on NL because the epidemiology and public health response to COVID-19 are regionally specific, vaccination and infection data are available for the NL population, and because we have estimated epidemiological quantities and reported key information for the COVID-19 pandemic in NL in our previous publications (Anokye et al, 2026; Doig et al, 2026; Hurford et al, 2023; Martignoni et al, 2023).

text.text: Studying this population helps generalize recommendations for future pandemic preparedness.

We develop an epidemiological model to implement counterfactual scenarios where booster dose administration: began earlier; occurred at a slower or faster rate; or occurred as it did in the Canadian population.
The Canadian rate scenario also assumes that the initial vaccination coverage is at either the NL or average Canadian levels.
The effects of no NPIs, strict NPIs and the actual NPIs are assessed in combination with the different vaccination scenarios.

We evaluate how vaccination affected the need for NPIs at the start of the Omicron wave in NL and determine the number of days that strict NPIs would need to be in place to achieve particular mitigation goals.
We calculate the number of hospitalizations and deaths that would have occurred in NL under each of these counterfactual scenarios.

We numerically solve a mechanistic Susceptible-Exposed-Asymptomatic-Infected-Recovered (SEAIR) model, previously developed by Anokye et al (2026), to quantify the impact of different combinations of vaccine administration and NPI implementation.

text.text: The exposed individuals transition to either the asymptomatic (A) or symptomatic (I) compartments after a latent period.
These individuals later recover and move on into the recovered compartment (R) where they remain immune to reinfection.
Our model stratifies the population of NL into three cohorts based on vaccination status after receiving a Health Canada-approved COVID-19 vaccine, without distinguishing between vaccine types.

The cohorts include unvaccinated individuals or those who have received one dose from a two-dose primary series (referred to as 'no primary series'), individuals who have completed the primary series (referred to as 'primary series'), and those who have one or more additional doses after receiving the primary series (referred to as 'booster doses').
Collectively, the 'no primary series' and 'primary series' cohorts are referred to as 'no booster doses'.
Individuals can transition from the no primary series cohort to the primary series cohort, and then from the primary series cohort to the booster dose cohort.
This assumption matches the definition of these vaccination statuses, for example that individuals must complete the primary vaccination series before receiving a booster dose.

The protection conferred by vaccination is modelled as a reduction in susceptibility to infection, and this is occurs through cohort-specific parameters (κ 1 , κ 2 , and κ 3 ) that contribute to the force of infection.
The model assumes vaccine-induced protection is immediate.
The original model diagram and parameterization are provided in Anokye et al (2026).

text.text: We assume only susceptible individuals in each vaccination cohort can receive vaccine doses and transition to another vaccination cohort.
We do not model vaccination for exposed, asymptomatic, or symptomatic individuals since few individuals with these states are likely to get vaccinated.

We do not model vaccination of recovered individuals because recovered individuals are assumed to be immune from infection, such that vaccination does not afford additional protection, and modelling the vaccination of recovered individuals is not likely to change our results.

text.text: The initial conditions for our simulations are the model variable values on December 15, 2021 and were determined by implementing a burn-in period of 150 days to enable the number of individuals in each state to approach equilibrium proportions.
The results we report consider the value of model variables from December 15, 2021 to December 15, 2022.
Our model is parameterized for the BA.1 Omicron variant.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the BA.2 variant replaced the BA.1 variant after a few months in NL.
Our simulations aim to understand the longterm impact of vaccination and NPI implementation on BA.1 spread under the hypothetical situation whereby BA.1 was not replaced by any other variants.

We assume no waning of immunity and the simulation period we have chosen is sufficiently long such that herd immunity is surpassed and any further infection that occurs contributes negligibly to the total number of infections.
The full system of equations and parameter estimates for our model are provided in the Supplementary Material.

The 'actual' vaccination scenario
In NL, booster doses were first offered on November 8, 2021 to people for whom at least six months had passed since their second dose (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, 2022).

Most of the NL population was ineligible at this time as only 9,673 people (≈ 1.9% of the NL population) met the necessary condition of at least 6 months since their second dose (Public Health Agency of Canada, 2026).

The administration of booster doses in NL accelerated substantially 35 days later (beginning December 13, 2021) when the required interval between receiving two vaccine doses was decreased to 22 weeks.
This change in eligibility meant that 154,100 people (≈ 30% of the NL population) were now eligible for booster doses.
We obtained weekly cumulative vaccination counts for NL and Canada from the Public Health Agency of Canada website (Public Health Agency of Canada, 2022, 2026).
These records include individuals who completed the primary (one or two dose) series and those who received additional booster doses.
First and second additional doses administered after the primary series were combined into a single booster category.
The vaccination data for NL had missing records for booster doses from the start date, 8 November 2021 to 7 February, 2022.

We interpolate these missing values by considering a report from the Newfoundland and Labrador Department of Health and Community Services (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, 2022), which stated that approximately 25% of eligible individuals in the province had received a booster dose by January 11, 2022 (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, 2022).

Therefore, 20.9% of the total NL population had received a booster doses by January 11 (see Figure 3B; marked as a red star) because the eligible population was individuals aged 12 years and older (426,198 individuals) and the total population of NL is 510,550 individuals.

Vaccination count data were reported as weekly aggregates and had constant values at some periods followed by sudden increases, which may be due to delayed reporting.
We smoothed the counts by redistributing later increases backward across the constant periods to correct the gaps and delayed reporting.

We converted these corrected weekly cumulative counts into a daily cumulative vaccination series using a monotone cubic-spline interpolation with an Hyman filter, and calculated daily rates as first differences of the interpolated cumulative series.

text.text: Our results suggest that all of these characteristics were important and acted together to reduce the number of hospitalizations and deaths that occurred in the year following the establishment of the Omicron variant in NL (Figure 6E) for a hypothetical scenario were the BA.1 variant continued to spread (without the emergence of the BA.2 variant) and assuming no waning of immunity.

text.text: NPIs are socially and economically disruptive (Clemente-Suárez et al, 2021; Koren and Pető, 2020; Mofijur et al, 2021) and when the Omicron variant established, residents were already fatigued from public health interventions that were implemented since the start of the pandemic two years earlier.

text.text: A reason why it would have been advantageous to start the booster dose vaccination rollout earlier in NL (blue line) or to administer vaccines at a 1.5 times faster rate (orange line) is that less stringent hospitalization targets, such as no more than 1,700 total hospitalizations or 25 peak daily hospital admissions, might have been met without any implementation of strict NPIs (Figure 7).

text.text: The actual booster dose administration strategy that occurred in NL was slower and later than our fast and early scenarios, but was still effective, in part, because NPIs were also implemented to delay infections and allow time for more people to receive booster doses before they were infected with the Omicron variant.

A limitation of our work is that we have not stratified infection risk, vaccination coverage, or the probability of hospitalization and death by age, gender, location, ethnicity, socio-economic status, or type of employment.

NL's population has the highest proportion of elderly people in Canada ( (Statistics Canada, 2021)), and so we expect that the projected number of hospitalizations and deaths would increase for all scenarios had a realistic age-structure been considered.

Immunocompromised people may be particularly vulnerable to infections, even when vaccinated, and are exposed to disproportionate risk when NPIs are suspended, while household members that experience domestic violence are exposed to disproportionate risk when 'stay-at-home' requirements are enacted.
An economic analysis might link the cost of NPIs and the cost of slow or late vaccination campaigns to identify an optimal combination of public health measures.

Our results contribute to this possible future direction as we use an epidemiologically-based method to quantify the hospitalizations and deaths for different vaccination and NPI scenarios to which the economic considerations might be added.

Additionally, we note that investment in vaccination campaigns, particularly ones that occur urgently, can divert resources from other branches of the healthcare system and a holistic analysis would also consider these factors.

Our simulations predicted that NL's high vaccination coverage prior to the establishment of the Omicron SARS-CoV-2 variant (81.3%) and booster dose vaccination campaign (resulting in 57.3% of NL's population receiving booster doses) reduced the number of hospitalizations occurring in Newfoundlanders and Labradorians in the next year by 519, and the number of deaths by 122 relative to a counterfactual scenario that implemented vaccination at the average Canadian rate (Figure 6E).

text.text: These reductions occurred, in part, because NL implemented some form of NPIs during the first 89 days after the Omicron variant established to offset the time that it took to administer booster doses.

We find that had the booster dose campaign in NL been implemented at half the actual rate (pink line), NPIs would need to have been enacted for a much longer period to achieve the same hospitalization targets (Figure 7).
